analysis.one_liner: Lets employers refuse to hire job applicants who work as union organizers.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let employers reject union organizer applicants, died in committee without ever getting a Senate vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the National Labor Relations Act, the main federal labor law, so that an employer could legally refuse to hire someone whose real purpose in applying is to organize the workforce. Unions use this tactic, called "salting," by sending paid organizers to apply for jobs at nonunion companies and build support for a union from inside. The bill would make that legal shield disappear: an employer could turn those applicants away without violating federal labor law.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, especially nonunion companies, would gain a new legal defense against a union organizing tactic. They could refuse to hire known or suspected union organizers without facing an unfair-labor-practice charge for discriminating based on union sympathy.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the National Labor Relations Act so that nothing in the employer unfair-labor-practice prohibitions requires an employer to hire a person who sought the job in furtherance of another employment or agency status [S2] [S3].

The bill's stated findings describe "salting" — paid union organizers applying for jobs to organize or inflict economic harm — as harassment that threatens the balance of labor-management rights [S3].
The bill's stated purpose is to relieve pressure on employers to hire people who seek employment to disrupt the workplace or inflict economic harm [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Union organizers and unions would lose one of their most effective tools for organizing nonunion workplaces, and workers at those companies would lose an inside path to forming a union. Job applicants generally would face a new employer defense that could be stretched to reject applicants perceived as union sympathizers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Unions and workers trying to organize

drawbacks.text: Critics of this type of bill argue that salting is a protected organizing strategy: it is often how workers at hostile nonunion employers learn about their legal right to form a union at all. Removing it removes a major route to union representation for workers who want one [S3 — the bill's own findings acknowledge the tactic targets nonunion employers].

The exception is written broadly — it covers anyone seeking employment "in furtherance of other employment or agency status" — which could be read beyond paid organizers to cover applicants with ties to advocacy or worker centers, creating a risk of lawful discrimination against union sympathizers generally [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For employers the benefit is real: it eliminates a tactic they see as covert and disruptive, and it would have given them a clear legal defense in labor disputes. The cost falls on workers' freedom to organize — one of the few methods unions have to reach nonunion workplaces — and the drafting leaves room for employers to screen out union sympathizers more broadly than the stated target. The bill weighed employers' control of hiring against workers' ability to organize, and came down on the employers' side.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate's labor committee, which never acted on it before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim DeMint introduced the bill on May 9, 2005, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S1] [S5] [S3].
No further action was taken — the bill received no committee markup, no floor vote, and no House counterpart action, and it expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1] [S5].
It had one cosponsor, a Republican senator [S4] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Unions and workers who might have organized nonunion workplaces are better off, because the bill never advanced. Employers who wanted the new hiring defense did not get it, but they also faced no change in the law's treatment of organizing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Unions and workers seeking to organize

for.name: Sen. Jim DeMint
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the single cosponsor were Republicans; no Democrat supported it and no organized opposition appears in the record, since the bill never left committee [S1] [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have given employers a legal right to reject applicants whose purpose is organizing, weakening a union tactic aimed at helping their employees unionize. The employer's gain here comes at the direct expense of workers' ability to organize.

Salting is one of the main ways unions reach workers at companies that resist organizing; the bill would have removed that tool. Unions' interest here runs with the workers they are trying to represent.
